clues.title: Google car: white hood, striped metal bars
text: This unique car was used for all street view coverage in the Dominican Republic. It can be recognized by the two metal bars, the **thick black stripes** on them, as well as the white hood visible at the front.
NOTE: These stripes can also be found on one of the Mongolian cars, but the landscape should allow you to tell them apart.
Within the Americas, you will also see metal bars in Guatemala and Curaçao. However, they will not have thick black stripes.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A white hood at the front and two metal roof bars with thick black stripes. Guatemala and Curaçao have similar bars but no thick stripes.

differs.how: Metal bars but no thick black stripes
Metal bars but no thick black stripes

clues.title: Pole: square concrete with reverse L top
text: Most electricity poles are **square and concrete**, with a reverse “L” shape at the top. Less commonly, round or octagonal poles are used.
NOTE: Within the Americas, only the Dominican Republic, Puerto Rico and Uruguay use square poles.

images.caption: A red arrow links a circled close-up of the concrete pole's top to the pole on the street

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Most electricity poles are square concrete with a reverse L shape at the top. In the Americas only Puerto Rico and Uruguay also use square poles.

clues.title: Plate: yellow top, white bottom
text: DR licence plates are somewhat reminiscent of New Jersey plates, being pale **yellow **at the top and **white **at the bottom.
NOTE: The Dominican Republic is the only part of Latin America, apart from Puerto Rico and Panama, where front plates are not required.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Plates are pale yellow on top and white below, a bit like New Jersey. Cars show no front plate, which only Puerto Rico and Panama also do in Latin America.

clues.title: Road: smooth, unusually dark asphalt
text: Roads in the Dominican Republic are often made of this **smooth** **asphalt**, which has a noticeably darker colour than in other countries.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Roads are often smooth asphalt that looks noticeably darker than in other countries.

clues.title: Sign: Spanish PARE stop, yellow posts
text: Despite being located in Central America, stop signs in DR contain the South American “PARE”. Moreover, many signs are attached to **yellow signposts**.
NOTE: ‘PARE’ is also used in all of South America as well as Puerto Rico.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Stop signs say PARE, the South American wording, and many signs sit on yellow posts. Puerto Rico and all of South America use PARE too.

clues.title: Coverage: only two cities
text: Street View coverage in the Dominican Republic is **very limited**. Only the capital Santo Domingo and the Northern city of Santiago de los Caballeros are covered.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Coverage is very limited. Only the capital, Santo Domingo, and the northern city of Santiago are covered.

clues.title: Landscape: mountains to the north
text: If you have **mountains to the North**, you will always be in Santiago de los Caballeros.
NOTE: Although some parts of Santo Domingo are hilly, you will never see proper mountains like this one.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: If you can see real mountains to the north, you are in Santiago. Some parts of Santo Domingo are hilly, but they never have mountains like this.

clues.title: Pole: yellow traffic light poles
text: **Yellow traffic light poles** are typically found in the city of Santiago de los Caballeros.
NOTE: This only applies to traffic light poles - yellow signposts are common in both cities.

images.caption: The traffic light hangs from a yellow pole at the roadside

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Yellow poles that hold traffic lights point to Santiago. Plain yellow signposts appear in both cities, so only the light poles count.

clues.title: City: tall buildings and wide avenues
text: As the capital and largest city, Santo Domingo has a **more developed downtown **area, with tall buildings and wide avenues.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A more developed downtown with tall buildings and wide avenues points to the capital, Santo Domingo.

clues.title: Sign: street names with the letters ADN
text: Street name signs in Santo Domingo often contain the letters **“ADN”**, a reference to the Distrito Nacional, which the city is located in.

images.caption: Green street name sign with the small letters ADN at the bottom left

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Street name signs often include the letters ADN. That is a short form of the national district around the capital, so it means Santo Domingo.

clues.title: Pole: black and purple markings
text: These **black-and-purple **pole markings are only found on poles in the Santo Domingo area.

images.caption: A concrete pole with black and purple painted marks and stickers

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Poles with black-and-purple painted markings are only found around the capital, Santo Domingo.

clues.title: Landscape: pale dirt, dry green scrub
text: This type of landscape is found on the outskirts of Santo Domingo. It is characterised by narrow dirt tracks, whitish dirt, **dried green shrubbery** and debris next to the road.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Narrow dirt tracks, whitish soil, dried green bushes and rubbish by the road. This look is found on the edges of the capital, Santo Domingo.

clues.title: Coverage: photos taken late in the evening
text: A small portion of the coverage in Santo Domingo was taken **late in the evening**. Similar imagery does not exist in Santiago de los Caballeros.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A small part of the capital's coverage was shot late in the evening. Santiago has no coverage like this, so a dusk image means Santo Domingo.
